# FROG README.md

# Summary

The main goal of this project is to rewrite the current Frequnecy Resolved Optical Gating (FROG) MATLAB script(s) in Python. In doing so, this will allow my lab much more usability, and the potential for much more usability of the files obtained from the spectrometer in the FROG setup. A chirped light pulse is a pulse that makes certain colors travel faster than others, ie. light of different frequencies arrive at different times relative to some detection device. The importance of this is after sending a collimated beam through a nonlinear crystal relative to the beams focus after traveling through a lens, we can chirp the light pulse(s), which spreads the frequencies out, ie. increases the bandwidth. Utilizing the FROG setup, we can then detect the bandwidth relative to the original and determine how much the beams bandwidth increased, which in turn lets us know the minimum length in time this light pulse can be. Overall, the FROG setup is a device that measures how much we've increased the bandwidth which then tells us how short we can make laser pulses in time. In Terahertz-Scanning Tunneling Microscopy (THz-STM), we rely on short pulses of light (In the THz frequency regime) to drive electrons across a tunnel junction (For us that includes the tungsten (W) STM tip (The probe), the gap separating the tip and the sample, and the sample itself). The shorter we can make these pulses, the better we can resolve the atomic structure of these samples in time. Overall, after the beam goes through the FROG setup and hits the spectrometer, we are given a few .M files with the main one giving us intensity vs. time of the beam. From here we get some very important results, with the main two being intensity vs. time and wavelength, as well as the relative phase vs. wavelength which can tell us a ton about our limitations when it comes to the individual pulses. 

The overall workflow doesn't have a ton of parts but there are 4 scripts that need to be rewritten: NewloadFrogTrace.m, FROGAnalysis.m, FROGAnalyzer.m, Quick_Graphing.m. The main work I have been doing up until now is just trying to understand MATLAB a bit better to get an understanding of what I am going to have to do Python function wise. Overall, I am still going to spend a bit of time with the overall understanding of individual components as I can read it enough to get what I need out of the scripts but the understanding aspect is still building. I am planning on beginning to rewrite the initial reading of the files into my version of NewloadFrogTrace.m, from here I will work on extracting the data from said files and utilizing them within my versions of FROGAnalysis.m and FROGAnalyzer.m. This is where majority of my time will be spent because I will need to thorughly go through interpolations, fourier transforms, and other mathematical (as well as estimations) that will result in accurate results. From there I will just need to write a plotting script from the outcomes as well as showcase given import values in optics such as the group delay dispersion (GDD). 

# Workflow

First two weeks: Continue working on understanding the matlab script, read in the files from the spectrometer via python, ideally begin on rewriting the analysis files. 

Essentially the rest of the project: Work through and organize everything in the analysis python code but make sure all of the equations are worked out correctly so that there isn't a domino effect of errors in calculations. Also, cross check the equations with the matlab code, ie. run sections of the matlab code so that every answer in the python code is double checked with the original code. 

Final week to two weeks: Rewrite the plotting software in python, and continuously test the completed files to ensure they are correct.
